about: The modern verified layer for A Text-Book of Astronomy (1903). Each entry names the book sentence(s) it judges (match: regular expressions that must find them — the build fails otherwise), what is established today, a status, and its sources. Status: Confirmed (still accepted as stated), Refined (right in substance, the value or understanding is now more exact), Superseded (replaced by a different understanding), Incorrect (shown wrong), Historically significant (a landmark the book records, still standing). Counts that keep changing (moons, asteroids) say 'as of' a date.

entries.topic: Distance of the sun (the astronomical unit)
match: very approximately 93,000,000 miles
entries.modern: The astronomical unit is fixed at exactly 149,597,870,700 metres — 92,955,807 miles. Measured today by radar ranging of the planets and spacecraft tracking.
sources: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 (re-definition of the astronomical unit)
entries.relationship: The book's 93,000,000 miles is within 0.05% of today's value. The method (Kepler's third law with the earth's mass) is sound; the precision is now far greater.

match: 186,337 miles per second
entries.modern: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second — 186,282.397 miles per second. Since 1983 it is a defined constant: the metre is defined from it.
sources: 17th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), 1983 — definition of the metre
entries.relationship: The book's figure is 55 miles per second (0.03%) too high — an excellent measurement for 1903, now replaced by an exact defined value.

entries.topic: Time light takes from the sun to the earth
match: light 8m\. 18s\. to come from the sun
entries.modern: Light takes 499.005 seconds — 8 minutes 19.0 seconds — to cross one astronomical unit.
entries.relationship: One second longer than the book's 8m. 18s.; the book's number came from the timing of Jupiter's satellites, which is less exact than radar ranging.

entries.topic: The light year in astronomical units
match: 63,368 radii of the earth's orbit
entries.modern: One light year (a Julian year of 365.25 days at the speed of light) is 63,241.08 astronomical units — 9.4607 × 10^12 km. Astronomers now mostly use the parsec (3.2616 light years).
sources: IAU Style Manual / IAU recommendations on units
entries.relationship: The book's 63,368 is 0.2% too large because its light time (8m. 18s.) was a second short.

match: Centauri, is 25,000,000,000,000 miles away
is 4\.26 years
entries.modern: Alpha Centauri A and B are 4.37 light years away (about 25.7 trillion miles). Their faint companion Proxima Centauri, found in 1915, is closer: 4.2465 light years (24.9 trillion miles) — the nearest star to the sun.
entries.value: Proxima Centauri 4.2465 ly; Alpha Centauri A/B 4.37 ly
sources: R. T. A. Innes, discovery of Proxima Centauri, 1915 (Circular of the Union Observatory)
entries.relationship: The book's distance is right to about 3%; the star it names is no longer the nearest, because Proxima was discovered twelve years after the book.

match: absolute temperature of the sun's surface 5,400° C
entries.modern: The sun's effective (surface) temperature is 5,772 K (about 5,500 °C).
entries.relationship: The book's 5,400 on the absolute scale is 7% low; the method (the wavelength of peak radiation — Wien's law, called Paschen's law here) is the one still taught.

match: the corona is not hot
entries.modern: The corona is extremely hot: 1 to 3 million kelvin, hundreds of times hotter than the surface below it. Shown in 1939–1943, when Grotrian and Edlén identified its green and red lines as iron atoms stripped of 13 and 9 electrons.
sources: B. Edlén, Zeitschrift für Astrophysik 22 (1943) — identification of the coronal lines
NASA Parker Solar Probe mission pages — https://www.nasa.gov/content/goddard/parker-solar-probe
entries.relationship: The book itself calls this result 'curious and at present unconfirmed' — rightly: it was wrong. Why the corona is so hot is still being studied by the Parker Solar Probe.
entries.why_then: The corona's light is faint and partly reflected sunlight; with the instruments of 1900 its measured 'effective temperature' came out low, and no one yet knew that its spectral lines came from extremely ionised iron, the tell-tale of millions of degrees.

match: progressive shrinking and compression of its molecules
entries.modern: The sun shines by nuclear fusion: in its core hydrogen is turned into helium, converting about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy every second (E = mc²). Contraction could keep it shining only tens of millions of years; the sun is 4.6 billion years old.
sources: H. A. Bethe, 'Energy Production in Stars', Physical Review 55 (1939)
A. S. Eddington, 'The Internal Constitution of the Stars' (1920)
Solar neutrinos detected: Davis (1968), confirmed by Super-Kamiokande and SNO (2001–2002)
entries.relationship: Replaced. Contraction (Helmholtz–Kelvin) is real but supplies far too little energy for the sun's true age.
entries.why_then: In 1903 no source of energy other than gravity was known that could be large enough. Radioactivity had only been discovered in 1896, Einstein's E = mc² came in 1905, and nuclear fusion was not understood until the 1930s. Gravitational contraction was the best physics of the day, and it gave an age that seemed long enough.

match: family of nine satellites
entries.modern: Saturn has 274 known moons (as of March 2025), the most of any planet, most of them small irregular moons a few kilometres across, found with large telescopes and the Cassini spacecraft.
sources: IAU Minor Planet Center announcements, March 2025
entries.relationship: The book's 'nine' (the ninth, Phoebe, photographed in 1898) was the full count then; it is now a tiny fraction. 'More than any other planet' still holds.

match: This is called the fifth satellite
entries.modern: Jupiter has 95 officially recognised moons (as of 2023), and more are being found.
entries.relationship: The book knew five: the four Galilean moons and Barnard's fifth (Amalthea, 1892).

match: Uranus has four satellites
one satellite which Neptune possesses
entries.modern: Uranus has 28 known moons and Neptune 16 (as of 2024). Neptune's large moon Triton does orbit backwards, as the book says.
entries.relationship: The counts were complete for 1903; the retrograde motion of Neptune's satellite is confirmed.

match: about 500 of them known
entries.modern: More than 1.3 million minor planets are known (Minor Planet Center, 2024), most in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter, with thousands of near-Earth asteroids tracked for safety.
sources: NASA Center for Near Earth Object Studies — https://cneos.jpl.nasa.gov/
entries.relationship: 'New ones are still found every year' is the part that stood: survey telescopes now find thousands a month.

match: canals are artificial water courses
^It is a remarkable feature of the canals
entries.modern: There are no canals on Mars. The lines were an optical illusion: the eye joins faint, unrelated markings at the limit of vision. Spacecraft from Mariner 4 (1965) and Mariner 9 (1971–72, the first full map) found craters, volcanoes and dry river valleys — but no canals.
entries.relationship: The book is cautious — it calls the artificial-canal idea 'wild speculation' made 'half in jest' — and that caution was justified.
entries.why_then: At the limit of a telescope's vision, in shimmering air, faint spots really do seem to line up; respected observers (Schiaparelli, Lowell) mapped the lines for decades, and no photograph was sharp enough to settle it until spacecraft reached Mars.

match: Like Venus, its rotation period is uncertain
entries.modern: Mercury rotates once every 58.65 days — exactly two rotations for every three orbits (88 days each), so it does not always turn the same face to the sun. Venus rotates backwards once every 243 days. Both were found by radar in the 1960s.
entries.value: Mercury 58.646 days (3:2 resonance); Venus 243.0 days, retrograde
sources: G. H. Pettengill & R. B. Dyce, Nature 206 (1965) — radar rotation of Mercury
NASA Mercury and Venus fact sheets — https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/
entries.relationship: The book rightly called the period uncertain; the 'balance of probability' it favoured (88 days, one face to the sun) turned out wrong.
entries.why_then: Mercury's faint markings are hard to see, and it is best observed at similar points of its orbit; because of the 3:2 resonance it shows nearly the same face each time, which looked like an 88-day rotation.

match: Neptune, the outermost planet of the solar system
entries.modern: Neptune is still the outermost planet. Pluto, found in 1930 and long counted as a ninth planet, has been classed since 2006 as a dwarf planet, one of many bodies in the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune.
sources: IAU 2006 Resolution B5 (definition of a planet)
C. Tombaugh, discovery of Pluto, Lowell Observatory, 1930
entries.relationship: Stated in 1903, doubted from 1930 to 2006, confirmed again by the IAU's definition of a planet.

entries.topic: The discovery of Neptune from the perturbations of Uranus
match: This working backward from the perturbations experienced by Uranus
entries.modern: Neptune was found on 23 September 1846 by Galle, within about 1° of the position Le Verrier calculated from Uranus' perturbations (Adams had made a similar calculation). It remains the classic triumph of Newtonian gravitation.
sources: U. J. Le Verrier, Comptes Rendus 23 (1846)
entries.relationship: As the book says: one of the greatest scientific achievements; the same method is used today to infer unseen bodies.

match: The law of gravitation is certainly a far-reaching one
entries.modern: Newton's law holds to high accuracy for most of the solar system, but Einstein's general relativity (1915) is the more exact theory: it explains the extra 43 arc-seconds per century in Mercury's perihelion, the bending of starlight (1919 eclipse) and the timing corrections GPS satellites need.
entries.value: General relativity (Einstein, 1915); Mercury perihelion +43″ per century
sources: A. Einstein, Sitzungsberichte der Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (1915)
Dyson, Eddington & Davidson, Philosophical Transactions A 220 (1920) — 1919 eclipse
entries.relationship: Right as the book uses it; refined, not replaced — Newton's law is the limit of relativity for weak gravity and slow motion.

entries.topic: Mass of the sun compared with the earth
entries.modern: The sun is 332,946 times as massive as the earth (1.989 × 10^30 kg).
entries.relationship: The book's 333,000 agrees to 0.02%.

match: _R_ is the radius of the earth, 3,963 miles
entries.modern: The earth's equatorial radius is 6,378.137 km (3,963.19 miles); the polar radius is 21 km less.
entries.relationship: Agrees to a fraction of a mile.

match: known distance of the moon \(240,000 miles\)
entries.modern: The moon's mean distance is 384,400 km (238,855 miles), measured to centimetres by bouncing lasers off reflectors left by Apollo astronauts and Soviet rovers since 1969.
sources: Lunar Laser Ranging (Apache Point / McDonald Observatory)
entries.relationship: The book's round 240,000 miles is within 0.5%.

match: mass of the earth is 81 times as great as the mass of the moon
entries.modern: The earth is 81.30 times as massive as the moon.
entries.relationship: Agrees.

entries.topic: Does the moon have an atmosphere?
match: if it has one at all its density is les
entries.modern: The moon has only an exosphere — a trace of gas about 10^-14 of the earth's atmosphere — measured by Apollo instruments and NASA's LADEE orbiter (2013–14).
entries.value: Exosphere only (~10^-14 of Earth's atmospheric density)
entries.relationship: The book's careful wording — not 'no atmosphere', but at most an extremely thin one — is exactly right.

match: a little more than eleven years
entries.modern: The sunspot cycle averages about 11 years and varies from about 9 to 14. Since Hale's discovery of sunspot magnetism (1908) it is known to be half of a 22-year magnetic cycle, in which the sun's magnetic poles swap.
sources: G. E. Hale, Astrophysical Journal 28 (1908) — magnetic fields in sunspots
NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center — solar cycle progression
entries.relationship: Confirmed and deepened: the cause is magnetic.

entries.topic: The Milky Way as a spiral, with the sun near its centre
match: Milky Way itself may be a gigantic spiral nebula near whose center lies the sun
entries.modern: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy about 100,000 light years across — but the sun is far from its centre: about 26,000 light years out, in a spiral arm. The centre holds a black hole of 4 million solar masses (Sagittarius A*).
entries.value: Sun ≈ 26,000 ly (8.2 kpc) from the galactic centre
sources: H. Shapley, Astrophysical Journal 48 (1918) — the sun off-centre, from globular clusters
GRAVITY Collaboration, Astronomy & Astrophysics 625 (2019) — distance to the galactic centre
Nobel Prize in Physics 2020 (Genzel, Ghez) — Sagittarius A*
entries.relationship: Half right: the spiral form was correct (and the book flags it as 'pure hypothesis'); the sun near the centre was wrong.
entries.why_then: Dust in the plane of the Milky Way dims distant stars equally in every direction along it, so star counts made the sun look central. Shapley moved the centre in 1918 using globular clusters, which can be seen above and below the dust.

entries.topic: Are there other systems of stars beyond ours?
match: little direct evidence that other such systems exist
all efforts at determining the parallax of either seem hopeless
entries.modern: The 'spiral nebulae' are other galaxies. In 1923–25 Edwin Hubble found Cepheid variable stars in the Andromeda nebula and showed it lies far outside the Milky Way — 2.5 million light years away. The observable universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies.
sources: E. P. Hubble, 'Cepheids in Spiral Nebulae', The Observatory 48 (1925)
entries.relationship: The book was right that parallax could never reach them; the distance came from a different yardstick (Cepheid stars), which was not yet known.
entries.why_then: No method could measure their distance in 1903: their parallax is far too small, and the Cepheid period–luminosity law (Leavitt) was published only in 1912.

match: The nebular hypothesis of Laplace has inclined astronomers
entries.modern: Planets form in flat disks of gas and dust around young stars — the solar nebula model, a descendant of Laplace's idea. Such protoplanetary disks are now seen directly (Hubble Space Telescope 1990s; ALMA's image of HL Tauri, 2014), and over 5,000 planets of other stars are known.
entries.relationship: The core idea survives; the details (rings thrown off by a shrinking sun) were replaced by accretion in a disk.

match: Roche's limit = 2\.44
entries.modern: Roche's limit is still used: a fluid moon held together only by its own gravity is torn apart inside about 2.44 planet radii × (density ratio)^1/3. Saturn's rings lie inside it, and comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 was torn apart by Jupiter in 1992 before striking it in 1994.
entries.relationship: Unchanged.
